claim: CD4+ DCs highly express EBI2
source: Here we show that CD4+ DCs highly express EBI2 and migrate to its oxysterol ligand, 7α,25-OHC.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing GFP fluorescence in EBI2-GFP reporter mice (Figure 1A), qPCR showing higher Ebi2 transcripts in CD4+ vs CD8+ DCs (Figure 1B), and surface staining showing higher EBI2 expression on CD4+ DCs (Figure 1C)

claim: CD4+ DCs migrate to the oxysterol ligand 7α,25-OHC
source: Here we show that CD4+ DCs highly express EBI2 and migrate to its oxysterol ligand, 7α,25-OHC.
evidence: Demonstrated by transwell chemotaxis assays showing CD4+ DCs migrate strongly to subnanomolar concentrations of 7α,25-OHC (Figure 1D)

claim: In mice lacking EBI2, CD4+ DCs are reduced in frequency
source: In mice lacking EBI2 or the enzymes needed for generating normal distributions of 7α,25-OHC, CD4+ DCs are reduced in frequency and the remaining cells fail to situate in marginal zone bridging channels.
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis shows threefold to fourfold deficiency in splenic CD4+ DCs in EBI2-deficient mice (Figure 1E,F)

claim: In mice lacking enzymes needed for generating normal distributions of 7α,25-OHC, CD4+ DCs are reduced in frequency
source: In mice lacking EBI2 or the enzymes needed for generating normal distributions of 7α,25-OHC, CD4+ DCs are reduced in frequency and the remaining cells fail to situate in marginal zone bridging channels.
evidence: Flow cytometry shows comparable selective loss of CD4+ DCs in Ch25h−/−, Cyp7b1−/−, and Hsd3b7−/− mice (Figure 1G)

claim: CD4+ DCs in EBI2-deficient mice fail to situate in marginal zone bridging channels
source: In mice lacking EBI2 or the enzymes needed for generating normal distributions of 7α,25-OHC, CD4+ DCs are reduced in frequency and the remaining cells fail to situate in marginal zone bridging channels.
evidence: Immunohistochemistry shows 33D1+ DCs are markedly underrepresented in bridging channels in EBI2-deficient mice and instead distributed in red pulp or T zone (Figure 3A)

claim: The CD4+ DC deficiency can be rescued by LTβR agonism
source: The CD4+ DC deficiency can be rescued by LTβR agonism.
evidence: Treatment with LTβR agonistic antibody for 6 days led to significant rescue in the proportion of CD4+ DCs in the spleen (Figure 5B,C)

claim: EBI2-mediated positioning in bridging channels promotes DC encounter with blood-borne particulate antigen
source: EBI2-mediated positioning in bridging channels promotes DC encounter with blood-borne particulate antigen.
evidence: Flow cytometry shows marked capture of PKH26+ SRBC by CD4+ DCs in wild-type mice, with marked deficiency in EBI2-deficient mice (Figure 6A,B)

claim: Upon exposure to antigen, CD4+ DCs move rapidly to the T-B zone interface
source: Upon exposure to antigen, CD4+ DCs move rapidly to the T-B zone interface and promote induction of helper T cell and antibody responses.
evidence: Immunohistochemistry shows SRBC injection led to very rapid movement of 33D1+ DCs from bridging channels to the T zone with notable bias for positioning at the B-T zone interface (Figure 6C)

claim: CD4+ DCs promote induction of helper T cell and antibody responses
source: Upon exposure to antigen, CD4+ DCs move rapidly to the T-B zone interface and promote induction of helper T cell and antibody responses.
evidence: EBI2-deficient mice show significant defect in OTII T cell proliferation following SRBC-Ova immunization (Figure 7A) and marked reduction in Hy10 B cell responses including plasma cells and germinal center B cells (Figure 7D,E)

claim: CD8− DCs from EBI2-GFP reporter mice show high GFP abundance compared to CD8+ DCs
source: CD11c+ splenic DCs from EBI2-GFP reporter mice showed high GFP abundance in CD8− vs CD8+ DCs (Figure 1A).
evidence: Flow cytometric detection of GFP fluorescence in gated splenic CD11c+MHCII+ cells from Ebi2GFP/+ mice (Figure 1A)

claim: CD4+ DCs from wild-type mice have more Ebi2 transcripts than CD8+ DCs
source: In agreement with the pattern of reporter expression, CD4+ DCs from wild-type mice had more Ebi2 transcripts than CD8+ DCs, and CD4+ DCs had higher surface expression of EBI2 (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Quantitative PCR analysis of Ebi2 transcript abundance in sorted splenic CD4+ and CD8+ DCs (Figure 1B)

claim: CD4+ DCs have higher surface expression of EBI2 than CD8+ DCs
source: In agreement with the pattern of reporter expression, CD4+ DCs from wild-type mice had more Ebi2 transcripts than CD8+ DCs, and CD4+ DCs had higher surface expression of EBI2 (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: EBI2 surface staining of gated splenic CD4+ and CD8+ DCs from Ebi2−/− or Ebi2+/+ mice (Figure 1C)

claim: The higher EBI2 expression in CD4+ DCs confers a strong ability to chemotax in response to 7α,25-OHC
source: The higher EBI2 expression in CD4+ DCs conferred a strong ability to chemotax in response to 7α,25-OHC in transwell assays, with the cells exhibiting migratory responses to subnanomolar concentrations of ligand (Figure 1D).
evidence: Transwell migration assays showing CD4+ DCs migrate to subnanomolar concentrations of 7α,25-OHC (Figure 1D)

claim: CD4+ DCs exhibit migratory responses to subnanomolar concentrations of 7α,25-OHC
source: The higher EBI2 expression in CD4+ DCs conferred a strong ability to chemotax in response to 7α,25-OHC in transwell assays, with the cells exhibiting migratory responses to subnanomolar concentrations of ligand (Figure 1D).
evidence: Migration assay data showing CD4+ DCs respond to 0.1 nM and higher concentrations of 7α,25-OHC (Figure 1D)

claim: CD8+ DCs fail to migrate to subnanomolar 7α,25-OHC
source: By contrast, CD8+ DCs failed to migrate to subnanomolar ligand and migration was weak even at high ligand concentrations (Figure 1D).
evidence: Migration assay data showing CD8+ DCs do not respond to subnanomolar concentrations and show weak migration even at high concentrations (Figure 1D)

claim: CD8+ DC migration to 7α,25-OHC is weak even at high ligand concentrations
source: By contrast, CD8+ DCs failed to migrate to subnanomolar ligand and migration was weak even at high ligand concentrations (Figure 1D).
evidence: Migration assay data showing CD8+ DCs have minimal migration even at 100 nM 7α,25-OHC (Figure 1D)

claim: EBI2-deficient mice have no change in the number of CD8+ DCs
source: Analysis of DC subsets in EBI2-deficient mice revealed a threefold to fourfold deficiency in splenic CD4+ DCs without a change in the number of CD8+ DCs or DN DCs (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Flow cytometry enumeration showing no significant difference in CD8+ DC numbers between Ebi2−/− and control mice (Figure 1F)

claim: EBI2-deficient mice have no change in the number of DN DCs
source: Analysis of DC subsets in EBI2-deficient mice revealed a threefold to fourfold deficiency in splenic CD4+ DCs without a change in the number of CD8+ DCs or DN DCs (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Flow cytometry enumeration showing no significant difference in DN DC numbers between Ebi2−/− and control mice (Figure 1F)

claim: When Cyp7b1-deficient mice are reconstituted with wild-type bone marrow, the mice remain CD4+ DC deficient
source: When Cyp7b1-deficient mice were reconstituted with wild-type bone marrow, the mice remained CD4+ DC deficient, indicating that radiation resistant stromal cells were a necessary source of EBI2 ligand (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Flow cytometry of Cyp7b1−/− recipients reconstituted with WT bone marrow showing continued CD4+ DC deficiency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)

claim: Radiation resistant stromal cells are a necessary source of EBI2 ligand
source: When Cyp7b1-deficient mice were reconstituted with wild-type bone marrow, the mice remained CD4+ DC deficient, indicating that radiation resistant stromal cells were a necessary source of EBI2 ligand (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Inference from bone marrow chimera experiment showing CD4+ DC deficiency persists when only stromal cells lack Cyp7b1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)

claim: The C-type lectin DCIR2 is present on all CD4+ DCs
source: The C-type lectin DCIR2, detected with the 33D1 antibody (Witmer and Steinman, 1984; Dudziak et al., 2007), is present on all CD4+ DCs and on a fraction of DN DCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing 33D1 expression on gated splenic DC subsets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)

claim: DCIR2 is present on a fraction of DN DCs
source: The C-type lectin DCIR2, detected with the 33D1 antibody (Witmer and Steinman, 1984; Dudziak et al., 2007), is present on all CD4+ DCs and on a fraction of DN DCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing 33D1 expression on gated splenic DC subsets including DN DCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)

claim: Enumeration of 33D1+ DCs shows a significant reduction in EBI2-deficient mice
source: Enumeration of 33D1+ DCs showed a significant reduction of positive cells in the spleen, confirming that the reduction in CD4+ DCs is due to a loss of this cell type rather than being due to a reduction in surface marker expression (Figure 1F).
evidence: Flow cytometry enumeration showing reduced 33D1+ DC numbers in Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 1F)

claim: The reduction in CD4+ DCs in EBI2-deficient mice is due to a loss of this cell type rather than a reduction in surface marker expression
source: Enumeration of 33D1+ DCs showed a significant reduction of positive cells in the spleen, confirming that the reduction in CD4+ DCs is due to a loss of this cell type rather than being due to a reduction in surface marker expression (Figure 1F).
evidence: Inference from 33D1+ DC enumeration data confirming cell loss rather than marker downregulation (Figure 1F)

claim: CD4+ DCs remaining in EBI2-deficient mice exhibit normal expression of MHC class II, CD80, CD83 and CD86
source: The CD4+ DCs remaining in EBI2-deficient mice exhibited normal expression of the surface molecules MHC class II, CD80, CD83 and CD86 and in vitro they supported a normal mixed lymphocyte reaction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing similar expression levels of MHCII, CD86, CD83, and CD80 on CD4+ DCs from Ebi2+/− and Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D)

claim: CD4+ DCs from EBI2-deficient mice support a normal mixed lymphocyte reaction in vitro
source: The CD4+ DCs remaining in EBI2-deficient mice exhibited normal expression of the surface molecules MHC class II, CD80, CD83 and CD86 and in vitro they supported a normal mixed lymphocyte reaction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: In vitro assay showing sorted CD4+ DCs from Ebi2−/− mice support similar T cell proliferation as controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E)

claim: A similar reduction in 33D1+ DCs is detected in peripheral (inguinal) lymph nodes of EBI2-deficient mice
source: Although the DC populations present in LNs are more heterogeneous than within spleen, we detected a similar reduction in 33D1+ DCs in peripheral (inguinal) and mucosal (mesenteric) LNs, while CD8+ DCs and migratory DCs were present at normal frequencies (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: Flow cytometry enumeration showing reduced 33D1+ DCs in inguinal LNs of Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 1H)

claim: A similar reduction in 33D1+ DCs is detected in mucosal (mesenteric) lymph nodes of EBI2-deficient mice
source: Although the DC populations present in LNs are more heterogeneous than within spleen, we detected a similar reduction in 33D1+ DCs in peripheral (inguinal) and mucosal (mesenteric) LNs, while CD8+ DCs and migratory DCs were present at normal frequencies (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: Flow cytometry enumeration showing reduced 33D1+ DCs in mesenteric LNs of Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 1I)

claim: CD8+ DCs are present at normal frequencies in lymph nodes of EBI2-deficient mice
source: Although the DC populations present in LNs are more heterogeneous than within spleen, we detected a similar reduction in 33D1+ DCs in peripheral (inguinal) and mucosal (mesenteric) LNs, while CD8+ DCs and migratory DCs were present at normal frequencies (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: Flow cytometry enumeration showing normal CD8+ DC numbers in LNs of Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 1H,I)

claim: Migratory DCs are present at normal frequencies in lymph nodes of EBI2-deficient mice
source: Although the DC populations present in LNs are more heterogeneous than within spleen, we detected a similar reduction in 33D1+ DCs in peripheral (inguinal) and mucosal (mesenteric) LNs, while CD8+ DCs and migratory DCs were present at normal frequencies (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: Flow cytometry enumeration showing normal migratory DC numbers in LNs of Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 1H,I)

claim: LN 33D1+ DCs express high amounts of EBI2
source: As in the spleen, LN 33D1+ DCs expressed high amounts of EBI2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing GFP fluorescence in gated lymph node DCs from Ebi2GFP/+ mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F)

claim: EBI2 is required intrinsically in CD4+ DCs
source: To test whether EBI2 was required intrinsically in CD4+ DCs we generated Ebi2−/− CD45.2: WT CD45.1 mixed BM chimeras. This analysis revealed a similar reduction in CD4+ DCs to that seen in fully deficient mice, establishing an intrinsic role for EBI2 in these cells and showing that the phenotype was not increased when the mutant cells had to compete with wild-type cells (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Mixed bone marrow chimera experiment showing selective reduction of Ebi2−/− CD4+ DCs compared to wild-type CD4+ DCs in the same host (Figure 2A,B)

claim: The CD4+ DC deficiency phenotype in EBI2-deficient cells is not increased when mutant cells compete with wild-type cells
source: To test whether EBI2 was required intrinsically in CD4+ DCs we generated Ebi2−/− CD45.2: WT CD45.1 mixed BM chimeras. This analysis revealed a similar reduction in CD4+ DCs to that seen in fully deficient mice, establishing an intrinsic role for EBI2 in these cells and showing that the phenotype was not increased when the mutant cells had to compete with wild-type cells (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Mixed bone marrow chimera showing similar magnitude of CD4+ DC reduction as in fully deficient mice (Figure 2A,B)

claim: All other splenic DC subsets, including pDCs, are unaffected by EBI2-deficiency
source: All other splenic DC subsets, including pDCs, were unaffected by EBI2-deficiency (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing normal frequencies of CD8+ DCs, DN DCs, and pDCs in mixed bone marrow chimeras (Figure 2A,B)

claim: Overexpression of EBI2 leads to a marked increase in the frequency of DCs in the spleen
source: 8 weeks post reconstitution there was a marked increase in the frequency of DCs in the spleens of mice overexpressing EBI2 and this increase was restricted to the 33D1+ DC subset (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Flow cytometry of mice reconstituted with EBI2-overexpressing bone marrow showing increased frequency of 33D1+ DCs (Figure 2C,D)

claim: The increase in DC frequency from EBI2 overexpression is restricted to the 33D1+ DC subset
source: 8 weeks post reconstitution there was a marked increase in the frequency of DCs in the spleens of mice overexpressing EBI2 and this increase was restricted to the 33D1+ DC subset (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing selective increase in 33D1+ DCs but not other DC subsets in EBI2-overexpressing mice (Figure 2C,D)

claim: EBI2 is necessary for development or maintenance of CD4+33D1+ DC
source: These data indicate that EBI2 is necessary for development or maintenance of CD4+33D1+ DC and elevated expression of EBI2 is sufficient to promote increased accumulation of this DC type.
evidence: Inference from mixed bone marrow chimera data showing intrinsic requirement for EBI2 in CD4+ DCs (Figure 2A,B)

claim: Elevated expression of EBI2 is sufficient to promote increased accumulation of CD4+33D1+ DCs
source: These data indicate that EBI2 is necessary for development or maintenance of CD4+33D1+ DC and elevated expression of EBI2 is sufficient to promote increased accumulation of this DC type.
evidence: Retroviral overexpression experiment showing increased 33D1+ DC frequency in EBI2-transduced cells (Figure 2C,D)

claim: 33D1+ DCs are concentrated in bridging channels of control mice
source: Strikingly, while 33D1+ DCs were concentrated in bridging channels of control mice, they were markedly under represented in these regions in EBI2-deficient mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry of spleen sections showing 33D1+ DCs concentrated in bridging channels in Ebi2+/− mice (Figure 3A)

claim: 33D1+ DCs are markedly underrepresented in bridging channels in EBI2-deficient mice
source: Strikingly, while 33D1+ DCs were concentrated in bridging channels of control mice, they were markedly under represented in these regions in EBI2-deficient mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry of spleen sections showing 33D1+ DCs are underrepresented in bridging channels in Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 3A)

claim: The 33D1+ DCs remaining in EBI2-deficient mice are mostly distributed in the red pulp or in the T zone
source: Although the total number of 33D1+ DCs in the sections was reduced, consistent with the reduced cell numbers detected by flow cytometry, the 33D1+ DCs that remained were mostly distributed in the red pulp or in the T zone (Figure 3A).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing 33D1+ DCs in red pulp and T zone rather than bridging channels in Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 3A)

claim: The distribution of DEC205+ DCs is unaltered in EBI2-deficient mice
source: The distribution of DEC205+ DCs was unaltered in EBI2-deficient mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing similar DEC205+ DC distribution in Ebi2+/− and Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 3B)

claim: A similar deficit of 33D1+ DCs in bridging channels is seen in Ch25h−/− mice
source: A similar deficit of 33D1+ DCs in bridging channels was seen in Ch25h−/−, Cyp7b1−/− and Hsd3b7−/− mice (Figure 3A) confirming the need for correctly distributed 7α,25-OHC to mediate 33D1+ DC positioning.
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing reduced 33D1+ DCs in bridging channels in Ch25h−/− mice (Figure 3A)

claim: A similar deficit of 33D1+ DCs in bridging channels is seen in Cyp7b1−/− mice
source: A similar deficit of 33D1+ DCs in bridging channels was seen in Ch25h−/−, Cyp7b1−/− and Hsd3b7−/− mice (Figure 3A) confirming the need for correctly distributed 7α,25-OHC to mediate 33D1+ DC positioning.
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing reduced 33D1+ DCs in bridging channels in Cyp7b1−/− mice (Figure 3A)

claim: A similar deficit of 33D1+ DCs in bridging channels is seen in Hsd3b7−/− mice
source: A similar deficit of 33D1+ DCs in bridging channels was seen in Ch25h−/−, Cyp7b1−/− and Hsd3b7−/− mice (Figure 3A) confirming the need for correctly distributed 7α,25-OHC to mediate 33D1+ DC positioning.
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing reduced 33D1+ DCs in bridging channels in Hsd3b7−/− mice (Figure 3A)

claim: Correctly distributed 7α,25-OHC is needed to mediate 33D1+ DC positioning
source: A similar deficit of 33D1+ DCs in bridging channels was seen in Ch25h−/−, Cyp7b1−/− and Hsd3b7−/− mice (Figure 3A) confirming the need for correctly distributed 7α,25-OHC to mediate 33D1+ DC positioning.
evidence: Inference from immunohistochemistry data showing similar positioning defects in all mice with altered 7α,25-OHC distribution (Figure 3A)

claim: 33D1+ DCs are situated most abundantly in areas between follicles in wild-type lymph nodes
source: Although 33D1+ DCs are less numerous in LNs, they were again situated most abundantly in areas between follicles in wild-type mice, and they were reduced in these regions in mice lacking EBI2 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry of lymph node sections showing 33D1+ DCs in interfollicular regions in Ebi2+/− mice (Figure 3C)

claim: 33D1+ DCs are reduced in interfollicular regions in lymph nodes of mice lacking EBI2
source: Although 33D1+ DCs are less numerous in LNs, they were again situated most abundantly in areas between follicles in wild-type mice, and they were reduced in these regions in mice lacking EBI2 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry of lymph node sections showing reduced 33D1+ DCs in interfollicular regions in Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 3C)

claim: Each subset of splenic DCs turns over at similar rates in EBI2-deficient and control mice
source: To examine the basis for the reduced numbers of CD4+ DCs in EBI2-deficient mice we first examined DC turnover rates using bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) incorporation. These measurements showed that each subset of splenic DCs turned over at similar rates in EBI2-deficient and control mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: BrdU incorporation assay showing similar turnover rates for CD4+ and CD8+ DCs in Ebi2+/− and Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 4A)

claim: When Cyp7b1-deficient mice are reconstituted with Bim−/− bone marrow, they continue to suffer a CD4+ DC deficiency despite having more total DCs
source: Splenic DCs are short-lived (Kamath et al., 2002) and their viability can be prolonged by removal of the proapoptotic molecule Bim (Chen et al., 2007). However, when Cyp7b1-deficient mice were reconstituted with Bim−/− BM, despite having more total DCs, they continued to suffer a CD4+ DC deficiency (Figure 4B).
evidence: Flow cytometry of Cyp7b1−/− mice reconstituted with Bim−/− bone marrow showing continued CD4+ DC deficiency (Figure 4B)

claim: More rapid apoptosis does not account for the reduced numbers of CD4+ DCs in mice lacking EBI2
source: These observations suggest that more rapid apoptosis does not account for the reduced numbers of CD4+ DCs in mice lacking EBI2 function.
evidence: Inference from Bim−/− rescue experiment and lack of differences in annexin V+ and active Caspase-3+ DCs

claim: EBI2 is expressed in pre-DCs at somewhat lower levels than in CD4+ DCs
source: EBI2 is expressed in pre-DCs though at somewhat lower levels than in CD4+ DCs (Figure 4C).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing GFP fluorescence in gated splenic pre-DCs from Ebi2GFP/+ mice (Figure 4C)

claim: EBI2-deficient mice contain normal numbers of pre-DCs in bone marrow and spleen
source: However, EBI2-deficient mice contained normal numbers of pre-DCs in BM and spleen (Figure 4D).
evidence: Flow cytometry enumeration showing similar pre-DC numbers in Ebi2+/− and Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 4D)

claim: When wild-type pre-DCs are transferred to Cyp7b1−/− recipients, the number of CD4+ DCs generated is reduced
source: When WT pre-DCs were transferred to Cyp7b1−/− recipients, the number of CD4+ DCs generated was reduced, consistent with the need for EBI2 ligand to sustain these DCs (Figure 4E).
evidence: Flow cytometry of pre-DC transfer experiment showing reduced CD4+ DC generation in Cyp7b1−/− recipients (Figure 4E)

claim: When Cyp7b1−/− pre-DCs are transferred to wild-type recipients, normal numbers of CD4+ DCs are generated
source: By contrast, when Cyp7b1−/− pre-DCs were transferred to wild-type recipients, normal numbers of CD4+ DCs were generated (Figure 4F).
evidence: Flow cytometry of pre-DC transfer experiment showing normal CD4+ DC generation from Cyp7b1−/− pre-DCs in wild-type recipients (Figure 4F)

claim: Cyp7b1−/− spleens contain a normal compartment of pre-DCs
source: These data demonstrate that Cyp7b1−/− spleens contain a normal compartment of pre-DCs and indicate that EBI2 is required in DCs after their differentiation to a CD4+ state.
evidence: Inference from pre-DC transfer experiments showing normal developmental potential of Cyp7b1−/− pre-DCs (Figure 4F)

claim: EBI2 is required in DCs after their differentiation to a CD4+ state
source: These data demonstrate that Cyp7b1−/− spleens contain a normal compartment of pre-DCs and indicate that EBI2 is required in DCs after their differentiation to a CD4+ state.
evidence: Inference from pre-DC transfer experiments showing normal pre-DC function but requirement for EBI2 ligand in recipient environment (Figure 4E,F)

claim: When Ebi2−/− and Ebi2+/− pre-DCs are cotransferred into wild-type hosts, fewer Ebi2−/− CD4+ DCs are detectable 6 days later
source: In further support of this conclusion, when sorted congenically distinguishable and violet tracer labeled pre-DCs from Ebi2−/− and Ebi2+/− mice were cotransferred into wild-type hosts, fewer Ebi2−/− CD4+ DCs were detectable 6 days later but these cells appeared to have divided a similar number of times as the control cells (Figure 4G,H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Flow cytometry of mixed pre-DC transfer showing reduced frequency of Ebi2−/− CD4+ DCs (Figure 4G)

claim: Ebi2−/− CD4+ DCs generated from transferred pre-DCs divide a similar number of times as control cells
source: In further support of this conclusion, when sorted congenically distinguishable and violet tracer labeled pre-DCs from Ebi2−/− and Ebi2+/− mice were cotransferred into wild-type hosts, fewer Ebi2−/− CD4+ DCs were detectable 6 days later but these cells appeared to have divided a similar number of times as the control cells (Figure 4G,H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing similar frequency of CD4+ DCs that had divided three or more times between Ebi2−/− and Ebi2+/− (Figure 4H)

claim: CD4+ DCs remaining in Ebi2−/− mice have similar amounts of the Notch induced gene ESAM as controls
source: CD4+ DC development is strongly dependent on Notch signaling (Caton et al., 2007; Lewis et al., 2011). Flow cytometric analysis showed that the CD4+ DC remaining in Ebi2−/− mice had similar amounts of the Notch induced gene, ESAM, as in controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing similar ESAM expression on CD4+ DCs from Ebi2+/− and Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)

claim: EBI2-deficient CD4+ DCs express similar amounts of the Notch target gene Deltex1 (Dtx1) as controls
source: They also expressed similar amounts of the Notch target gene Deltex1 (Dtx1) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Quantitative PCR showing similar Dtx1 transcript levels in CD4+ DCs from Ebi2+/− and Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)

claim: EBI2-deficient CD4+ DCs have normal levels of the IRF4 target Mmp12
source: IRF4 is another factor important for development of splenic CD4+ DCs (Tamura et al., 2005) but EBI2-deficient CD4+ DCs had normal levels of the IRF4 target Mmp12 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that this transcription factor had been appropriately activated.
evidence: Quantitative PCR showing similar Mmp12 transcript levels in CD4+ DCs from Ebi2+/− and Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)

claim: Inoculation with Flt3 ligand producing cells leads to expansion of both CD4+ and CD8+ DCs in control mice
source: Flt3 ligand plays a role in the development and maturation of most splenic DC types (Hashimoto et al., 2011). To test if diminished access to Flt3 ligand might account for the reduction in CD4+ DCs mice were inoculated with Flt3 ligand producing cells. This led to the expected expansion of both CD4+ and CD8+ DCs in control mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing increased CD4+ and CD8+ DCs in Ebi2+/− mice inoculated with Flt3-ligand expressing cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D)

claim: Flt3 ligand treatment expands DCs in EBI2-deficient mice but the selective deficiency in CD4+ DCs remains
source: There was also expansion of DCs in the EBI2-deficient mice, but the selective deficiency in CD4+ DCs remained (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing DC expansion but continued CD4+ DC deficiency in Ebi2−/− mice treated with Flt3-ligand (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D)

claim: Insufficient access to Notch ligand, Flt3 ligand or GM-CSF cannot explain the reduced numbers of CD4+ DCs in EBI2-deficient mice
source: These data suggest that insufficient access to Notch ligand, Flt3 ligand or GM-CSF cannot explain the reduced numbers of CD4+ DCs.
evidence: Inference from experiments showing normal Notch signaling markers and failure of Flt3-ligand or GM-CSF to rescue CD4+ DC deficiency

claim: LTα1β2 is important for homeostasis of splenic CD4+ DCs
source: Another factor that is important for homeostasis of splenic CD4+ DCs is the cytokine LTα1β2 (Kabashima et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: Citation of previous studies showing LTα1β2 importance for CD4+ DC homeostasis

claim: When mice lack LTα1β2, CD4+ DCs are reduced in number and the level of LTβR on the cells is elevated
source: In previous work we found that when mice lacked LTα1β2 not only were CD4+ DCs reduced in number, but the level of LTβR on the cells was elevated, consistent with less ligand-mediated down-modulation (Kabashima et al., 2005).
evidence: Citation of previous work showing CD4+ DC reduction and elevated LTβR in LTα1β2-deficient mice

claim: LTβR is elevated on CD4+ DCs in EBI2-deficient mice
source: Flow cytometric analysis of cells from EBI2-deficient mice revealed elevation of LTβR on the remaining CD4+ DCs while there was minimal change in the LTβR surface levels on CD8+ DCs (Figure 5A).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing increased LTβR surface staining on CD4+ DCs from Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 5A)

claim: There is minimal change in LTβR surface levels on CD8+ DCs in EBI2-deficient mice
source: Flow cytometric analysis of cells from EBI2-deficient mice revealed elevation of LTβR on the remaining CD4+ DCs while there was minimal change in the LTβR surface levels on CD8+ DCs (Figure 5A).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing similar LTβR surface staining on CD8+ DCs from Ebi2+/+ and Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 5A)

claim: Treatment with LTβR agonistic antibody for 6 days leads to a significant rescue in the proportion of CD4+ DCs in EBI2-deficient spleens
source: Consistent with the DC-deficiency being a consequence of reduced LTβR signaling, treatment for 6 days with an LTβR agonistic antibody (De Trez et al., 2008; Stanley et al., 2011) led to a significant rescue in the proportion of CD4+ DCs present in the spleen (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing increased percentage of CD4+ DCs in Ebi2−/− mice treated with LTβR agonist antibody (Figure 5B,C)

claim: After LTβR agonist treatment, increased numbers of EBI2-deficient 33D1+ DCs are evident in both the T zone and red pulp but not in the bridging channels
source: In tissue sections, increased numbers of EBI2-deficient 33D1+ DCs were evident in both the T zone and red pulp but not in the bridging channels (Figure 5D).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing 33D1+ DCs in T zone and red pulp but not bridging channels in LTβR agonist-treated Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 5D)

claim: A rescue in the proportion of CD4+ DCs is seen when Cyp7b1−/− mice are reconstituted with bone marrow from transgenic mice that overexpress LTα1β2 on B cells
source: A rescue in the proportion of CD4+ DCs was also seen when Cyp7b1−/− mice were reconstituted with BM from transgenic mice (Ngo et al., 2001) that overexpress LTα1β2 on B cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing increased CD4+ DC frequency in Cyp7b1−/− mice reconstituted with LTβ10 transgenic bone marrow (Figure 5E)

claim: EBI2-mediated positioning of CD4+ DCs between follicles and near LTα1β2-expressing B cells is required for maintenance of the CD4+ DC compartment
source: These data are consistent with the possibility that EBI2-mediated positioning of CD4+ DCs between follicles and near LTα1β2-expressing B cells (Ansel et al., 2000) is required for maintenance of the CD4+ DC compartment.
evidence: Inference from LTβR agonist rescue experiments and elevated LTβR on EBI2-deficient CD4+ DCs

claim: Flow cytometric analysis reveals marked capture of PKH26+ antigen by splenic CD4+ DCs 1 day after SRBC injection
source: To explore this idea we injected mice intravenously with sheep red blood cells (SRBCs) that had been labeled with the membrane dye, PKH26 (Hagnerud et al., 2006). 1 day later, flow cytometric analysis revealed marked capture of PKH26+ antigen by splenic CD4+ DCs whereas capture by CD8+ DCs was considerably lower (Figure 6A).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing high frequency of PKH26+ CD4+ DCs compared to CD8+ DCs after SRBC-PKH26 injection (Figure 6A)

claim: Antigen capture by CD8+ DCs is considerably lower than by CD4+ DCs after SRBC injection
source: 1 day later, flow cytometric analysis revealed marked capture of PKH26+ antigen by splenic CD4+ DCs whereas capture by CD8+ DCs was considerably lower (Figure 6A).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing lower frequency of PKH26+ CD8+ DCs compared to CD4+ DCs (Figure 6A)

claim: A similar extent of antigen capture by CD4+ DCs is evident as early as 30 min after SRBC injection
source: A similar extent of antigen capture by CD4+ DCs was evident as early as 30 min after SRBC injection and PKH26+ CD4+ DCs were still evident in the spleen at 48 hr (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing PKH26+ CD4+ DCs at 0.5 hr after SRBC-PKH26 injection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A)

claim: PKH26+ CD4+ DCs are still evident in the spleen at 48 hr after SRBC injection
source: A similar extent of antigen capture by CD4+ DCs was evident as early as 30 min after SRBC injection and PKH26+ CD4+ DCs were still evident in the spleen at 48 hr (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing PKH26+ CD4+ DCs at 48 hr after SRBC-PKH26 injection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)

claim: There is a marked deficiency in the number of PKH26 antigen+ DCs in EBI2-deficient mice compared to wild-type
source: Comparison of the number of PKH26 antigen+ DCs between wild-type and EBI2-deficient mice showed a marked deficiency in the latter (Figure 6B).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing reduced number of PKH26+ total DCs and CD4+ DCs in Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 6B)

claim: SRBC injection leads to very rapid movement of 33D1+ DCs from bridging channels to the T zone
source: Remarkably, SRBC injection led to very rapid movement of 33D1+ DCs from bridging channels to the T zone, with a notable bias for positioning at the B-T zone interface (Figure 6C).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing 33D1+ DCs at T-B zone interface 3 hr and 1 day after SRBC immunization (Figure 6C)

claim: SRBC-activated 33D1+ DCs show a notable bias for positioning at the B-T zone interface
source: Remarkably, SRBC injection led to very rapid movement of 33D1+ DCs from bridging channels to the T zone, with a notable bias for positioning at the B-T zone interface (Figure 6C).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing 33D1+ DCs concentrated at B-T zone interface after SRBC immunization (Figure 6C)

claim: 33D1+ DCs remain at the T-B zone interface for 1 day after SRBC injection
source: The cells remained in this location for 1 day, but by 2 days the distribution of 33D1+ DCs resembled more closely the unstimulated state (Figure 6C).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing 33D1+ DCs at T-B zone interface at day 1 after SRBC immunization (Figure 6C)

claim: By 2 days after SRBC injection, the distribution of 33D1+ DCs resembles more closely the unstimulated state
source: The cells remained in this location for 1 day, but by 2 days the distribution of 33D1+ DCs resembled more closely the unstimulated state (Figure 6C).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing 33D1+ DC distribution at day 2 resembling unstimulated pattern (Figure 6C)

claim: The inward movement of 33D1+ DCs following SRBC immunization occurs more rapidly than following injection with LPS
source: Interestingly, the inward movement of 33D1+ DCs following SRBC immunization occurred more rapidly than following injection with LPS and with a greater bias for the T-B boundary (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry comparing 33D1+ DC positioning after SRBC vs LPS immunization at 3 hr and 6 hr (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E)

claim: 33D1+ DC movement following SRBC immunization shows greater bias for the T-B boundary than following LPS injection
source: Interestingly, the inward movement of 33D1+ DCs following SRBC immunization occurred more rapidly than following injection with LPS and with a greater bias for the T-B boundary (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing 33D1+ DCs concentrated at T-B boundary after SRBC but more distributed in T zone after LPS (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E)

claim: When mice are pretreated with unlabeled SRBCs for 6 hr to promote DC movement into the T zone and then injected with PKH26+ SRBC, the extent of PKH26+ antigen capture by CD4+ DCs is selectively diminished
source: Confirming the importance of bridging channel positioning in favoring access to blood-borne antigen, when mice were pretreated with unlabeled SRBCs for 6 hr to promote DC movement in to the T zone and then injected with PKH26+ SRBC, the extent of PKH26+ antigen capture by CD4+ DCs was selectively diminished (Figure 6D).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing reduced PKH26+ CD4+ DC frequency in mice pretreated with unlabeled SRBC (Figure 6D)

claim: CCR7 is upregulated on CD4+ DCs within 1.5 hr of SRBC injection
source: To define the basis for the rapid repositioning of antigen-engaged DCs we tested whether the cells underwent changes in EBI2 or CCR7 expression. CCR7 was upregulated within 1.5 hr of SRBC injection (Figure 6E) and the cells responded more vigorously to the CCR7 ligands CCL21 and CCL19 than cells from saline injected mice (Figure 6F).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing increased CCR7 surface staining on CD4+ DCs 1.5 hr after SRBC immunization (Figure 6E)

claim: CD4+ DCs respond more vigorously to CCR7 ligands CCL21 and CCL19 after SRBC injection than cells from saline injected mice
source: CCR7 was upregulated within 1.5 hr of SRBC injection (Figure 6E) and the cells responded more vigorously to the CCR7 ligands CCL21 and CCL19 than cells from saline injected mice (Figure 6F).
evidence: Transwell migration assay showing increased CD4+ DC migration to CCL21 and CCL19 after SRBC immunization (Figure 6F)

claim: EBI2 expression and function is minimally affected following SRBC injection
source: By contrast, EBI2 expression and function was minimally affected following SRBC injection (Figure 6F and not shown).
evidence: Migration assay showing similar CD4+ DC migration to 7α,25-OHC before and after SRBC immunization (Figure 6F)

claim: Injection of SRBC fails to cause DC mobilization from MZ bridging channels to the T-B boundary when mice are reconstituted with CCR7-deficient bone marrow such that most CD4+ DCs are CCR7-deficient
source: When mice were reconstituted with a mixture of CCR7-deficient and EBI2-deficient BM such that the majority of CD4+ DCs were CCR7-deficient while most other cell types were CCR7 wild-type, injection of SRBC failed to cause DC mobilization from MZ bridging channels to the T-B boundary (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F), confirming the role of CCR7 in this repositioning event.
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing 33D1+ DCs remain in bridging channels after SRBC immunization in mice with CCR7-deficient DCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F)

claim: When EBI2-deficient mice that received wild-type OTII T cells are immunized with Ova-conjugated SRBCs, there is a significant defect in the extent of T cell proliferation
source: Finally we examined how the reduced CD4+ DC frequency and defective DC positioning in EBI2-deficient mice affected CD4 T cell and T-dependent B cell responses. When EBI2-deficient mice that had received wild-type ovalbumin (Ova)-specific OTII TCR transgenic T cells were immunized with Ova-conjugated SRBCs there was a significant defect in the extent of T cell proliferation (Figure 7A).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing reduced OTII T cell proliferation in Ebi2−/− mice after SRBC-OVA immunization (Figure 7A)

claim: OTII T cells responding in EBI2-deficient mice show less strong upregulation of ICOS and PD1
source: The responding T cells also showed less strong upregulation of ICOS and PD1 (Figure 7A).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing reduced ICOS and PD1 expression on OTII cells in Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 7A)

claim: CD4 T cell proliferation following injection with soluble Ova is unaffected by EBI2-deficiency
source: This defect appeared to be selective to responses against particulate antigen as CD4 T cell proliferation following injection with soluble Ova or 33D1 antibody conjugated with Ova (Dudziak et al., 2007) was unaffected by EBI2-deficiency (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing similar OTII T cell proliferation in Ebi2+/− and Ebi2−/− mice after soluble OVA immunization (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B)

claim: CD4 T cell proliferation following injection with 33D1 antibody conjugated with Ova is unaffected by EBI2-deficiency
source: This defect appeared to be selective to responses against particulate antigen as CD4 T cell proliferation following injection with soluble Ova or 33D1 antibody conjugated with Ova (Dudziak et al., 2007) was unaffected by EBI2-deficiency (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing similar OTII T cell proliferation in Ebi2+/− and Ebi2−/− mice after 33D1-OVA immunization (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C)

claim: Hy10 B cells undergo reduced proliferation in EBI2-deficient hosts 3 days after HEL-SRBC immunization
source: To test for effects on induction of a T-dependent antibody response, EBI2-deficient or control mice were given transfers of wild-type HEL-specific Hy10 B cells and then immunized with HEL-SRBC. 3 days later the Hy10 B cells had undergone reduced proliferation in EBI2-deficient compared to control hosts (Figure 7B).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing reduced Hy10 B cell proliferation in Ebi2−/− mice 3 days after SRBC-HEL2x immunization (Figure 7B)

claim: At day 5 after HEL-SRBC immunization, there is an approximately 14-fold reduction in total plasma cells in EBI2-deficient hosts
source: When the Hy10 B cell response in EBI2-deficient hosts was examined at day 5, there was an ∼14-fold reduction in total plasma cells and a ∼7-fold reduction in germinal center B cells (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing reduced total plasma cell numbers in Ebi2−/− mice at day 5 (Figure 7D,E)

claim: At day 5 after HEL-SRBC immunization, there is an approximately 7-fold reduction in germinal center B cells in EBI2-deficient hosts
source: When the Hy10 B cell response in EBI2-deficient hosts was examined at day 5, there was an ∼14-fold reduction in total plasma cells and a ∼7-fold reduction in germinal center B cells (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing reduced germinal center B cell numbers in Ebi2−/− mice at day 5 (Figure 7D,E)

claim: Isotype switched (IgG1 and IgG2b) plasma cells are more strongly affected (15- to 30-fold reduced) than IgM plasma cells (approximately 7-fold reduced) in EBI2-deficient mice
source: Analysis of isotype switched (IgG1 and IgG2b) plasma cell numbers showed they were more strongly affected (15- to 30-fold reduced) than IgM plasma cells (∼7-fold reduced, Figure 7D,E).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing greater reduction in IgG1+ and IgG2b+ plasma cells compared to IgM+ plasma cells in Ebi2−/− mice (Figure 7D,E)

claim: EBI2 function in DCs is needed for mounting normal CD4 T cell-dependent B cell responses
source: These findings provide strong evidence that EBI2 function in DCs is needed for mounting normal CD4 T cell-dependent B cell responses.
evidence: Inference from experiments showing defective T cell and B cell responses in EBI2-deficient mice and in chimeras where DCs are EBI2-deficient

claim: Splenic DCs are short-lived
source: Splenic DCs are short-lived (Kamath et al., 2002) and their viability can be prolonged by removal of the proapoptotic molecule Bim (Chen et al., 2007).
evidence: Citation of previous studies on DC lifespan and Bim function

claim: DC viability can be prolonged by removal of the proapoptotic molecule Bim
source: Splenic DCs are short-lived (Kamath et al., 2002) and their viability can be prolonged by removal of the proapoptotic molecule Bim (Chen et al., 2007).
evidence: Citation of Chen et al., 2007 study on Bim and DC viability

claim: The spleen is the largest secondary lymphoid organ
source: The spleen, the largest secondary lymphoid organ, has an essential function in supporting rapid B and T cell responses against circulating antigens (Mebius and Kraal, 2005).
evidence: Statement of established anatomical knowledge with citation

claim: The spleen has an essential function in supporting rapid B and T cell responses against circulating antigens
source: The spleen, the largest secondary lymphoid organ, has an essential function in supporting rapid B and T cell responses against circulating antigens (Mebius and Kraal, 2005).
evidence: Citation of Mebius and Kraal, 2005 on spleen function

claim: CD4+ 33D1+ DCs in the spleen are enriched in the marginal zone bridging channel
source: The CD4+ 33D1+ DCs in the spleen are enriched in an area of the white pulp known as the marginal zone (MZ) bridging channel, where the T zone abuts the blood-rich red pulp (Mitchell, 1973; Witmer and Steinman, 1984; Steinman et al., 1997).
evidence: Citation of previous studies showing CD4+ DC localization in bridging channels

claim: CD8+ DEC205+ DCs are mostly located within the T zone
source: CD8+ DEC205+ DCs, by contrast, are mostly located within the T zone (also known as the periarteriolar lymphatic sheath or PALS).
evidence: Statement of established DC localization pattern

claim: DCs derive from pre-DCs in the bone marrow
source: DCs derive from pre-DCs in the bone marrow (BM) and these cells seed the spleen and give rise to the CD4+, CD8+ and DN DC subsets (Naik et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2007).
evidence: Citation of Naik et al., 2006 and Liu et al., 2007 on DC development

claim: Pre-DCs seed the spleen and give rise to the CD4+, CD8+ and DN DC subsets
source: DCs derive from pre-DCs in the bone marrow (BM) and these cells seed the spleen and give rise to the CD4+, CD8+ and DN DC subsets (Naik et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2007).
evidence: Citation of Naik et al., 2006 and Liu et al., 2007 on pre-DC differentiation

claim: The transcription factors IRF2, IRF4, RelB and RBP-J are needed for CD4+ DC development
source: The transcription factors IRF2, IRF4, RelB and RBP-J are needed for CD4+ DC development whereas Batf3, IRF8 and Id2 are required for CD8+ DC development (Hashimoto et al., 2011; Satpathy et al., 2012).
evidence: Citation of Hashimoto et al., 2011 and Satpathy et al., 2012 on transcription factor requirements

claim: Batf3, IRF8 and Id2 are required for CD8+ DC development
source: The transcription factors IRF2, IRF4, RelB and RBP-J are needed for CD4+ DC development whereas Batf3, IRF8 and Id2 are required for CD8+ DC development (Hashimoto et al., 2011; Satpathy et al., 2012).
evidence: Citation of Hashimoto et al., 2011 and Satpathy et al., 2012 on transcription factor requirements

claim: CD4+ DCs require signaling by Notch to induce RBP-J
source: CD4+ DCs require signaling by Notch to induce RBP-J (Lewis et al., 2011), and by the cytokine LTα1β2, the latter coming from B cells (Kabashima et al., 2005).
evidence: Citation of Lewis et al., 2011 on Notch signaling in CD4+ DCs

claim: CD4+ DCs require signaling by the cytokine LTα1β2, which comes from B cells
source: CD4+ DCs require signaling by Notch to induce RBP-J (Lewis et al., 2011), and by the cytokine LTα1β2, the latter coming from B cells (Kabashima et al., 2005).
evidence: Citation of Kabashima et al., 2005 on LTα1β2 requirement for CD4+ DCs

claim: EBI2 (GPR183) is a Gαi coupled receptor that responds to the oxysterol ligand, 7α,25-hydroxycholesterol (OHC)
source: EBI2 (GPR183) is a Gαi coupled receptor that responds to the oxysterol ligand, 7α,25-hydroxycholesterol (OHC) (Hannedouche et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: Citation of Hannedouche et al., 2011 and Liu et al., 2011 on EBI2 ligand identification

claim: EBI2 is upregulated by activated B cells
source: EBI2 is upregulated by activated B cells and plays an important role in promoting their movement to inter- and outer-follicular regions of lymphoid organs during T-dependent antibody responses (Gatto et al., 2009; Pereira et al., 2009).
evidence: Citation of Gatto et al., 2009 and Pereira et al., 2009 on EBI2 in B cells

claim: EBI2 plays an important role in promoting activated B cell movement to inter- and outer-follicular regions of lymphoid organs during T-dependent antibody responses
source: EBI2 is upregulated by activated B cells and plays an important role in promoting their movement to inter- and outer-follicular regions of lymphoid organs during T-dependent antibody responses (Gatto et al., 2009; Pereira et al., 2009).
evidence: Citation of Gatto et al., 2009 and Pereira et al., 2009 on EBI2 function in B cell positioning

claim: 7α,25-OHC is synthesized from cholesterol by the actions of two enzymes, CH25H and CYP7B1
source: 7α,25-OHC is synthesized from cholesterol by the actions of two enzymes, CH25H and CYP7B1, and these are expressed at high levels by stromal cells in inter- and outer-follicular regions while expression of Ch25h is repressed in the center of follicles (Yi et al., 2012).
evidence: Citation of Yi et al., 2012 on 7α,25-OHC synthesis and distribution

claim: CH25H and CYP7B1 are expressed at high levels by stromal cells in inter- and outer-follicular regions
source: 7α,25-OHC is synthesized from cholesterol by the actions of two enzymes, CH25H and CYP7B1, and these are expressed at high levels by stromal cells in inter- and outer-follicular regions while expression of Ch25h is repressed in the center of follicles (Yi et al., 2012).
evidence: Citation of Yi et al., 2012 on enzyme expression patterns

claim: Expression of Ch25h is repressed in the center of follicles
source: 7α,25-OHC is synthesized from cholesterol by the actions of two enzymes, CH25H and CYP7B1, and these are expressed at high levels by stromal cells in inter- and outer-follicular regions while expression of Ch25h is repressed in the center of follicles (Yi et al., 2012).
evidence: Citation of Yi et al., 2012 on Ch25h expression pattern

claim: EBI2 is present on a variety of hematopoietic cell types, including DCs
source: As well as expression by B cells, EBI2 is present on a variety of other hematopoietic cell types, including DCs (Hannedouche et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: Citation of Hannedouche et al., 2011 and Liu et al., 2011 on EBI2 expression pattern
